AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: Pain at intrauterine contraception (IUC) fitting may be a deterrent for women and any reduction in discomfort would be likely to be beneficial to both women and clinicians.

AbstractText.Label: AIM
AbstractText.content: This study investigated the associated pain and the ease of use of two different stabilising forceps at the time of IUC placement.

AbstractText.Label: DESIGN
AbstractText.content: Single-blinded randomised controlled trial. One hundred parous women aged 18-50 years who had undergone at least one vaginal delivery were recruited.

AbstractText.Label: SETTING
AbstractText.content: An integrated sexual health service in the North of England.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: Women were randomised to the use of either a Littlewoods forceps or a single-toothed tenaculum forceps to stabilise the cervix at the time of IUC placement. Pain levels were measured at forceps application, IUC insertion, and 5 and 10 minutes post-procedure using a visual analogue scale (VAS). A clinician graded ease of use of the forceps and any associated bleeding. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were used to compare pain levels between the two forceps groups. Linear regression was used when adjusting for potential confounders.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Mean VAS scores were similar at forceps application (p=0.52), IUC fitting (p=0.10) and at 5 minutes (p=0.32). There was a statistical difference in the degree of pain experienced at 10 minutes in the tenaculum group (p=0.01). Physicians found both forceps easy to use and there was no difference in bleeding (p=0.49).

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Parous women who have had a vaginal delivery can be reassured that IUC fitting is well tolerated. Pain scores were not affected by the type of forceps used to stabilise the cervix at IUC placement. Both forceps investigated were easy to use.
